job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I read only the text you pasted, so these are drafting observations, not legal conclusions. Some items cut both ways: they let companies continue, or they expose the bill to challenge. Where I mention existing law, please verify the citation before publishing.

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **§2(1)(A), single-vessel threshold.** Only recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons by "a single vessel" counts. A fleet of vessels, each under the threshold, can recover far more in aggregate, and there is no aggregation or affiliated-entity rule.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" and "recovery."** The bill doesn't say whether the year is a calendar year, a rolling 12 months, or a license year. It also doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry, or measured at the seabed or on deck. Because the violation only occurs once the annual total is exceeded, it is unclear when it begins and how §5(a)'s daily penalties accrue.

3. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** Seabed-based or unmanned collection systems and fixed platforms that aren't vessels fall outside the definition, as do shore-based recovery systems. Activity can be restructured to avoid the vessel element.

4. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and the 200-meter line.** "Seabed," "deep," and "mineral resources" are undefined, and the depth measurement method and datum are unspecified. Read literally, the text could reach oil and gas, sand and gravel, dredging, or cable work deeper than 200 meters. That is a possible overbreadth challenge, and it also leaves it unclear whether sulfides, crusts, and brines are covered. Nothing addresses activity inside the U.S. EEZ or in territories.

5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The bill never defines which Secretary this is. Sec. 6 says "Secretary of State" explicitly, which makes the unqualified usage here more confusing.

6. **§2(1)(B), standardless authority.** "Risks… comparable to" is undefined. There is no rulemaking, notice, deadline, or review procedure, and no statement whether determinations apply only prospectively. Paired with §5(b)'s criminal penalty, this invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, joint ventures, permanent residents, and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. firms. "State" is also undefined, so DC and territories are unclear. A company could restructure offshore to fall outside it.

8. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross ton floor doesn't match the 10,000 ton recovery threshold, so a smaller vessel can exceed the threshold without ever registering. "Equipped for the recovery" is vague as applied to chartered or temporarily fitted vessels, and the gross tonnage measurement standard is unspecified.

## Prohibition and exemptions (Sec. 3)

9. **§3(a), "any person in the United States."** "Person" is undefined, so it is unclear whether it covers federal agencies, state entities, or foreign governments. "In the United States" is also undefined and may or may not reach the territorial sea, EEZ, or continental shelf. The bill doesn't say how it applies to foreign nationals on foreign-flag vessels in U.S. waters.

10. **§3(a), "engage in."** The bill doesn't reach financing, processing, transporting, selling, or importing seabed minerals, or supplying equipment. Minerals recovered abroad by non-U.S. persons can still enter the U.S. market, and there is no aiding-and-abetting language.

11. **§3(a), extraterritorial reach.** "Any U.S. person anywhere" has no enforcement mechanism: no boarding authority, flag-state coordination, or venue provision. Combined with the narrow §2(2) definition, foreign subsidiaries and foreign-flag vessels may escape it.

12. **§3(b), "exploration license" is undefined.** The bill doesn't say who must have issued it. A license from a foreign government or an international body that predates enactment could arguably qualify, exempting some U.S. persons.

13. **§3(b), unlimited grandfathering.** There is no cap on volume, area, or duration, and no expiration, and nothing addresses renewal, modification, extension, or transfer. Holders could continue indefinitely, and possibly expand or sell the license to someone else.

14. **§3(b), license type and pre-enactment timing.** Only "exploration" licenses are exempt, and exploration licenses usually don't authorize commercial recovery. That leaves it unclear how commercial-recovery permit holders and pending applicants are treated. Any license issued between now and enactment is also grandfathered, which creates an incentive to rush issuance. The lack of transition provisions invites takings and due process litigation.

15. **§3(c), environmental assessment.** The exemption turns on the "purpose" of the activity, with no volume cap, time limit, permit, notice requirement, or ban on selling or retaining recovered material. It could serve as a pretext for commercial-scale recovery. "Activities" is undefined.

## Timing (Secs. 5, 6, 7, 8)

16. **§5(a) vs. §8.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act, including §3, takes effect 180 days later. Defendants can argue no violation was possible in the gap, or challenge any attempt to penalize that period on fair-notice grounds.

17. **§8, the 180-day gap.** Nothing freezes new activity or licensing between enactment and the effective date. Operators can ramp up, and the bill has no wind-down or transition rule for activity that continues past the effective date.

18. **§§6, 7(b), clocks run from enactment.** Both clocks start at enactment, not the effective date, so the prohibition is actually in force for about 9.5 years, and the State Department's negotiation clock starts before the Act is operative.

## Enforcement (Secs. 3, 5)

19. **No designated enforcer (Secs. 3, 5).** The bill doesn't say which agency investigates violations, assesses civil penalties, or brings suit. It has no administrative hearing process, inspection, subpoena, seizure, or forfeiture authority, no rulemaking authority, and no authorization of appropriations.

20. **§5(a), penalty design.** "Not more than $1,000,000" per day has no assessment factors, notice-and-hearing procedure, or inflation adjustment. The daily accrual is ambiguous given the annual tonnage test, and an uncapped daily total invites an Excessive Fines challenge.

21. **§5(b), "willfully."** The bill doesn't say what must be willful: the conduct, knowledge of the tonnage, awareness of a Secretary determination under §2(1)(B), or knowledge of the law. Because the offense depends on a numeric threshold and a discretionary determination, defendants have an easy lack-of-knowledge argument. Venue for offenses at sea is also unaddressed.

22. **§5 doesn't reach §4.** There is no penalty for failing to register, failing to file reports, or filing false ones. Existing false-statement law may cover some false filings, but failure to file is uncovered.

23. **No citizen suit, review provision, or limitations period.** Without them, environmental groups can't sue to compel enforcement, and challenges to agency action proceed under general law. Default federal limitations periods will fill the gap.

## Registry (Sec. 4)

24. **§4(a), registration.** There is no deadline, no required registration contents, no renewal, and no process for denial or deregistration. "Operator" is undefined, and it's unclear whether foreign-flag vessels run by foreign entities must register.

25. **§4(b), reporting.** There is no due date and no required content: tonnage, location, depth, dates, and measurement method are unspecified. "Certified by the operator" is undefined, and there is no audit, verification, public access, or confidentiality rule. NOAA could not reliably test the annual tonnage threshold from what is filed.

26. **§4 isn't tied to the §3 exemptions.** Nothing requires operators claiming the (b) or (c) exemptions to identify the license or assessment basis, so exemptions are effectively self-declared.

## Duration and international provisions (Secs. 6, 7)

27. **§7(a), joint resolution mechanism.** The bill doesn't direct or fund the National Academies study or set a deadline for it, and there are no expedited procedures. "Serious harm" is undefined. A joint resolution is subject to presidential veto, and the text doesn't say that a finding actually terminates the prohibition.

28. **§7(a) vs. §7(b).** Subsection (a) implies the prohibition lasts until Congress finds mining safe, but (b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless of any finding. As written, (b) makes (a) largely irrelevant, and it is unclear which controls.

29. **§7(b), no savings clause.** Nothing preserves enforcement of violations committed before the sunset, so defendants may argue pending cases abate. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. §109) addresses repeal, and it isn't clear it covers expiration.

30. **§6, international agreement.** "Seek to negotiate" requires no outcome. "Equivalent" is undefined, and it's unclear whether "not later than 18 months" modifies the negotiating or the concluding. There is no reporting requirement to Congress or consequence for missing the deadline, and the bill doesn't say whether the agreement is a treaty requiring Senate consent.

## Cross-cutting

31. **Relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or preempt the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. ch. 26) or other seabed statutes. NOAA's existing licensing and permitting authority could conflict with the new prohibition.

32. **"Commercial" is a misnomer.** The definition is purely volume-based, with no sale or profit test. A nonprofit or government research operation above the threshold is covered, while a commercial operation below it is not. This mismatch with the title could cause confusion in litigation.

33. **No severability clause.** If §2(1)(B) or the criminal penalties were struck down for vagueness, the bill doesn't say whether the rest stands.

34. **No findings or constitutional basis.** The bill has no findings or purpose statement and doesn't identify its constitutional basis. That makes the extraterritorial reach harder to defend in court.

## Where I'd start at markup

For the most consequential items, I'd look first at 1 and 7 (easy structural workarounds), 12–15 (the grandfathering and assessment carve-outs), 16 and 17 (the timing gap), 19 (no enforcer), 6 (the Secretary's standardless authority), and 28 (the internal conflict in §7).

I can also turn this into a short explainer for the newsletter, or draft questions staff could put to committee aides and stakeholders, if that would help.
